evidence_quote: To be selected, schools (and their districts) had to serve high numbers of ELs ... In the selected schools, all eighth-grade social studies teachers participated, and their class sections were randomly assigned to the treatment or comparison condition.
resolved_title: Improving Content Knowledge and Comprehension for English Language Learners: Findings From a Randomized Control Trial (Journal of Educational Psychology, 2017, 109(1), 22-34)
notes: Recoded from the correct document; the text file is now the JEP article, not the online supplement. Schools and districts were chosen for high numbers of ELs, so the selection is on a non-achievement characteristic at the school level; within schools every eighth-grade social studies class and every student in it took part (ELs, former ELs, and English speakers; 26.7 percent EL), so no student rule and opt_in 0. The ellipsis in the quote omits the clause 'and each class had to have at least one identified EL', which is also a school or class level rule. The authors add that districts and principals ultimately decided which schools joined, giving EL shares of 15 to 45 percent, but the stated recruitment criterion stands. Kraft's single effect (0.40) is the full-sample content knowledge (ASK) effect reported for ELs and non-ELs together; WWC lists the finding sample as 1,236 students, which is smaller than the 1,405 with ASK posttests implied by the article's attrition figures, so the analytic count is unclear but the sample is the full one. WWC sample text agrees with the article and adds no eligibility rule.

evidence_quote: Stanford University's Education Program for Gifted Youth (EPGY) conducted a randomized-treatment experiment during the 2006-2007 school year to test the efficacy, for Title I students, of the technological and individualized EPGY Kindergarten through Grade 5 Mathematics Course Sequence, modified for the Title I schools.
resolved_title: Effectiveness of an Individualized Computer-Driven Online Math K-5 Course in Eight California Title I Elementary Schools
notes: Abstract only. Eight Title I elementary schools in three California districts; the study was framed as a test for Title I students and WWC confirms all participating schools were Title I, so selection on Title I status at the school level. No student-level rule stated. mixed_samples = 1 because the abstract restricts its reported effects to students in the top half of the distribution of correct first-exercise attempts (an engagement measure), and Kraft's effects (-0.04, 0.00; n 340 to 1144) do not match the substantial positive effects the abstract reports, so they likely come from a different (full-sample or WWC-recomputed) analysis. Abstract also describes matched control students despite calling the design a randomized-treatment experiment.

evidence_quote: Within participating schools, all pupils in Years 7, 9 and 11 were eligible for inclusion.
resolved_title: Texting Parents: Evaluation report and executive summary
notes: Full EEF report. Cluster RCT in 36 English secondary schools (29 analysed), randomised at the Key Stage group level; schools recruited through existing networks, with eligibility based on willingness to be randomised and provide data, not on need. Parents could opt out (285 did), so opt_in = 0. International setting (England), Years 7, 9 and 11 (ages 11 to 16). mixed_samples = 1 because Kraft lists ten effects with n_min = 664, which matches the free-school-meals subsample analysis (Table 11, p. 27; intervention n of 668 English and 678 maths), so some of Kraft's effects come from the FSM subgroup while others match the full-sample analytic n (11,587 maths).
